Hi!
I'm Vanda Miravent and I'm a new user of DISTANCE 3.5.

My study has the aim to estimate relative densities of song birds by
the method and statistical theory proposed by JŠrvinen and VŠisŠnen (
1975 in Oikos).
I understood that in this method they collect data field in transepts
with two belts: 0 to Y and  Y to infinity and to estimate the
detectability and density of a specie they use the proportion of birds
detected within the belt 0 to Y relatively to the total number  of
birds  detected in the two bands.

My question is:

- DISTANCE 3.5 allow to analise data collected in that way and estimate
densities  using that proportion of  birds detected in the two belts?

- If yes,  how to introduce data recorded in interval Y to infinity and
how to define its interval in the program

                                                            Thank  You ,

Vanda Miravent

messages.subject: Re: (no subject)
messages.body_plain:
> > My study has the aim to estimate relative densities of song birds by
> > the method and statistical theory proposed by JŠrvinen and VŠisŠnen (
> > 1975 in Oikos).
> > I understood that in this method they collect data field in transepts
> > with two belts: 0 to Y and  Y to infinity and to estimate the
> > detectability and density of a specie they use the proportion of birds
> > detected within the belt 0 to Y relatively to the total number  of
> > birds  detected in the two bands.
> >
> > My question is:
> >
> > - DISTANCE 3.5 allow to analise data collected in that way and estimate
> > densities  using that proportion of  birds detected in the two belts?

Yes - at least approximately.  You need to replace 'infinity' by some
large value w - and the analysis will probably be rather more robust if
you don't make that value too large.  Say w=100m for woodland/forest,
larger for more open habitat.

> > - If yes,  how to introduce data recorded in interval Y to infinity and
> > how to define its interval in the program

Just record them all at any distance larger than Y - say Y+1 m.  Then in
the 'intervals' tab of the data filter, define 2 intervals, one from 0 to
Y, the other from Y to w.  (Note: for distances in the 1st interval,
record them as any value between 0 and Y - say Y/2.)

Note that you will only be able to fit one-parameter models - the
half-normal without any adjustment terms, or the uniform with one
adjustment term - and you won't be able to test whether the model fits the
data with just 2 intervals.

Steve Buckland

messages.subject: Request for range finder advice
messages.body_plain:
I am interested in purchasing range finders for sampling animals from
gazelle fawn size (roughly dog sized) upwards at at least 1000m but have a
limited budget. Does anyone have any advice on models available and whether
they can pick up animals this small at such distances? I am based in the UK
so any advice on UK suppliers would be great (I have been chasing Bushnell
but it appears I can only see some if I buy them first!) Thanks in advance,

Tom Maddox

(Please could you cc. any suggestions to s.du...@ucl.ac.uk)

messages.subject: Help wanted: Spanish language users of Distance 3.5
messages.subject_clean: Help wanted: Spanish language users of Distance 3.5
messages.body_plain:
This message is for spanish language users of Distance 3.5.

If you are successfully running Distance 3.5 in a Spanish language version of
Windows 95 or 98 please can you send me a copy of a project file that you have
used in Distance?  It will help me diagnose a problem that some people are
having with Distance.  Please make sure that:

1. You are using a Spanish language version of Windows - not an English
Language version with Spanish regional settings.  You'll know if its the right
version if your start menu is called "Inicio" and your windows help ("Ayunda de
Windows") is in Spanish.

2. You have opened the distance project file and, say run at least one
analysis.  (You can use the sample files if you like)

3. You zip the project file up using Winzip or equivalent if possible before
you send it to me, so it's not too large.  Please tell me which version of
windows you're using.

Thanks!

 - Len Thomas

--
Len Thomas, Co-ordinator
Distance Development Project
Research Unit for Wildlife Population Assessment
Mathematical Institute, University of St Andrews
Scotland KY16 9SS

messages.subject: Feral goat abundance
messages.body_plain:
I'm about to begin my MSc research at the
University of Auckland, on the use of line transects
to estimate feral goat abundance in New Zealand
forests.  I have been told that there has been work
carried out on Deer in Scotland using permanent
"cable" transects. My methodology seems fine but
would like to review this information if possible.
As yet I have been unable to find this work in the
literauture, although I have seen a summary of work
on Deer in Scotland using indirect faecal pellet
counts in the RUWPA web page, i'm not sure if this
is the same one.  Can anyone help?
-----------------------------------------------
Dan Godoy
d.g...@auckland.ac.nz
The University of Auckland
Private Bag 92019,
Auckland,
New Zealand

messages.subject: Re: Feral goat abundance
messages.body_plain:
Dear Dan:

I have beed dong line transect surveys of ungulates in forested habitats
in in India (10 sites) for over a decade. Some of the data was published
in the following publications:

Karanth K. U. and Sunquist M. E. 1992.  Population structure, density
and biomass of large herbivores in the tropical forests of Nagarahole,
India.  Journal of Tropical Ecology 8: 21-35.

Karanth K. U. and Sunquist M. E.  1995.  Prey selection by tiger,
leopard and dhole in tropical forests. Journal of Animal Ecology 64:
439-450.

Karanth K. U. and Nichols J. D. 1998.  Estimating tiger densities in
India from camera trap data using photographic captures and recaptures.
Ecology 79 (8): 2852-2862.

Karanth K. U. and Stith B. M.  Prey depletion as a critical determinant
of tiger population viability. 1999. In Riding the Tiger: Tiger
conservation in human dominated landscapes (Editors: J. Seidensticker,
S. Christie and P. Jackson), Cambridge University Press (Pages 100-113).

Madhusudan M. D. and Karanth K. U. 2000.  Hunting for an answer: Local
hunters and large mammal conservation in India. In J. G. Robinson and E.
L. Bennett (editors), Hunting for sustainability in tropical forests.
Columbia University Press, New York.

Basically, I feel the LT method works well in forests, provided
densities of the target species are not too low in which case the
sampling effort needed to get >40 detection may become impractical.

UNIVERSITY OF KENT AT CANTERBURY
INSTITUTE OF MATHEMATICS AND STATISTICS

READER/SENIOR LECTURER/LECTURER IN STATISTICS

A Reader/Senior Lecturer/Lecturer post in Statistics in the Institute of
Mathematics and Statistics at the University of Kent at Canterbury is
available from 1 September 2000 or such a date as may be arranged.

Depending on the post applied for, the successful candidate will have a
strong research record or potential in an area of statistics or applied
probability and a commitment to excellence in teaching. Preference may be
given to a person who has proven expertise in at least one application
area and an ability to take advantage of advances in computation to
produce innovative modelling.

Informal enquiries should be directed to Professor Philip Brown, Tel: +44
(0)1227-823794 or Professor Byron Morgan, Tel: +44 (0)1227-827612 (direct
lines), Fax: +44 (0)1227-827932, E-mail: Philip....@ukc.ac.uk or
B.J.T....@ukc.ac.uk

Information about the Institute of Mathematics and Statistics may also be
found on the World Wide Web: http://www.ukc.ac.uk/ims/

Depending on the level of the appointment, salary will be in the range
17,238-38,561 pounds.

Please telephone the Personnel Office for Further Particulars on
01227-827837 (24 hours) or 01227-823674 (Minicom), quoting reference
A00/39
